Shifting sands: the regulatory landscape shaping large-load development globally

View Caitlin Connelly's full profile

Surging electricity demand is testing the limits of power market infrastructure across the world. Unprecedented large-load development is forcing stakeholders to rewrite the rules that define how to plan for growth, allocate costs and ensure there is power where it’s needed. 
Led by data centres, the speed and scale of large-load growth is a huge challenge for grid operators and utilities used to decades of flat electricity demand. As pressure on grids builds, the power sector landscape is evolving rapidly, seeking the right balance between speed to power, grid reliability and affordability.   
We recently invited key stakeholders including legislators, utilities and large-load customers to discuss how large loads are reshaping power sector policy and regulation. Fill out the form on this page to access the webinar recording and slides, and read on for an introduction to the themes dominating the global regulatory landscape. 
1. Interruptible service options and queue prioritisation 
Flexible service options are becoming commonplace in speed-to-power proposals. This approach enables utilities to provide services to large-load customers even when reliability cannot be fully guaranteed, either through voluntary or compulsory service interruptions.   
What are the potential obstacles for utilities to imposing interruptible service options? Watch the webinar to learn more. 
2. Large load tariffs and cost allocation methodologies 
These approaches aim to ensure large-load customers pay for the true costs involved in providing them with power, shielding existing customers from any financial impact. Cost allocation methodologies aim to isolate the specific grid upgrade costs attributable to the large-load customers driving them, so that these costs can be apportioned directly and proportionately.  
What legitimate objections do large-load customers have to cost allocation methodologies? Find out by watching the webinar. 
3. Efficiency compliance standards 
Regulatory oversight of data centres increasingly encompasses mandating the operational efficiency of the facility itself. Compliance is often being made a prerequisite for interconnection or zoning approval. This approach is a particular focus of regulators in Europe. 
4. Readiness-based interconnection criteria 
The roll-out of artificial intelligence is driving a huge increase in speculative data centre projects. To address interconnection backlogs, regulators are implementing rules aimed at ensuring only financially committed, ‘shovel-ready’ projects consume grid operator resources. 
Differences in approach between jurisdictions and a rapidly evolving political climate can encourage large-load customers to shop around for the best regulatory conditions and ‘hedge their bets’. Learn more in the webinar.
5. Siting standards and prioritisation 
Government regulators are beginning to use zoning to align new data centre development with national economic and digital sovereignty goals, with strategic ‘growth zones’ a key focus in Asia. Permitting processes are also undergoing increased consolidation across jurisdictions.
6. Treatment of co-located generation 
Siting a data centre directly at or close to a generation plant has become a popular strategy to pursue expedited interconnection. Large-load customers can also build their own onsite generation, or support the development of distributed resources and virtual power plants to help meet the demand they create. Reforms are emerging to clarify how this sort of behind-the-meter generation interacts with the grid.  
US utility PG&E aims to use large-load growth as a means to support the grid and improve overall affordability for its customers. Watch the webinar to learn more.
